summary: Specifies the Bootstrap Router (BSR) mechanism for PIM sparse-style multicast protocols. BSR is one way for a multicast router to learn the group-to-Rendezvous-Point mappings it needs in order to work. Candidate routers advertise themselves and an elected bootstrap router distributes the information. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: Multicast routers need to know which meeting-point router handles each group. BSR is a way to pick a leader that announces the list of meeting points to everyone.

questions: how do routers learn rendezvous points
how is the bootstrap router elected
subtitle: How multicast routers elect a leader that tells everyone which Rendezvous Point serves which group.

tldr.problem: Every router in a PIM domain must map a given multicast group address to the same Rendezvous Point (RP). Static configuration does not scale well and does not adapt to router or link failures.
tldr.mechanism: Candidate-BSRs elect one Bootstrap Router. Candidate-RPs send it advertisements, and it floods the chosen set of group-to-RP mappings to every router in Bootstrap messages.
tldr.outcome: BSR is dynamic, largely self-configuring and robust to router failure. RFC 5059 obsoletes RFC 2362 for this mechanism and extends it to work with administrative scoping. It has been updated by RFC 8736 and RFC 9436.

today: RFC 5059 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 2362 and updates RFC 4601. It has itself since been updated by RFC 8736 and RFC 9436, so read it together with those.

sections.title: The Problem: Finding the Rendezvous Point
sections.content:
In PIM Sparse Mode and Bidirectional PIM, every multicast group needs a Rendezvous Point (RP), whose address is the root of a distribution tree reaching every receiver of that group. For senders to reach all receivers, every router in the domain must use the same group-to-RP mappings. The PIM specifications do not mandate how routers learn them.

A router keeps its mappings in an RP-Set. Each mapping holds a group range (address and prefix length), an RP priority, an RP address, a hash mask length and an SM/BIDIR flag. Ranges may overlap, so a deterministic algorithm, defined by the routing protocol rather than by BSR, picks one RP for each group. PIM-SM uses a hash function when several RPs share the same priority.

The simplest solution is static configuration on every router, but it generally does not scale and does not adapt to failures, except when combined with Anycast-RP. The Bootstrap Router (BSR) mechanism creates viable mappings and distributes them quickly. It was first defined in RFC 2362, and this document gives an updated specification that also handles administratively scoped regions and different flavors of routing protocols.
sections.plainLanguage: Everyone must agree on which room hosts which club, or the club members never find each other. Writing the list by hand on every door is slow and breaks when a room closes.

sections.title: How BSR Works: Four Phases
sections.content:
Some routers are configured as Candidate-RPs (C-RPs) and some as Candidate-BSRs (C-BSRs). The mechanism has four phases, which in practice may all run at the same time.

  • BSR election. Each C-BSR originates Bootstrap messages (BSMs) carrying a BSR Priority. Routers flood them through the domain, and a C-BSR that hears of a better C-BSR stops sending its own for a while. The one left becomes the elected BSR.
  • C-RP advertisement. Each C-RP periodically sends Candidate-RP-Advertisement (C-RP-Adv) messages to the elected BSR, with its priority and the group ranges it offers.
  • RP-Set formation. The BSR picks a subset of the C-RPs. The set should be neither too big to distribute nor so small that load concentrates, and it should not change often.
  • RP-Set flooding. The BSR includes the RP-Set in future BSMs, which are flooded so the set reaches every router quickly. Routers add the mappings to those they already have from other sources, such as static configuration.

If the domain is partitioned, each part elects its own BSR. When it heals, a new election happens automatically. Some disruption in packet delivery is expected, lasting on the order of the region's round-trip time and the BS_Timeout value.

With administrative scoping, a separate copy of the mechanism runs inside each admin-scope zone, plus one non-scoped copy for the whole domain. Zone Border Routers (ZBRs) do not forward scoped traffic across the boundary, and scoped BSMs do not cross it either. Each zone needs at least one C-BSR and at least one C-RP for its addresses.
sections.plainLanguage: First the teachers pick a head teacher. Then the room owners tell the head teacher which rooms are free, and the head teacher shouts the final list to the whole school over and over.

sections.title: Electing the Bootstrap Router
sections.content:
BSMs serve both for election and for distributing the RP-Set. Each BSR has a weight: the BSR Priority field followed by the BSR's IP address, with the priority in the most-significant bits. The higher weight wins. For historical reasons the highest BSR priority is 255 (higher is better), while for an RP priority the best value is 0 (lower is better).

A Candidate-BSR is in one of three states per scope zone: Candidate-BSR (another router is currently preferred), Pending-BSR (no better router is known but this one is not yet elected; a temporary state that avoids thrashing) and Elected-BSR. The initial state is Pending-BSR, with the Bootstrap Timer set to BS_Rand_Override.

A router that is not a C-BSR is in NoInfo, Accept Any or Accept Preferred for each zone. In Accept Preferred it only accepts BSMs from the current BSR or from a C-BSR with a higher weight.

Before a BSM is considered at all, it must pass checks: it must come from a directly connected neighbor with active Hello state, be sent to ALL-PIM-ROUTERS, and (unless it has the No-Forward bit) come from the correct RPF neighbor toward the BSR. It must also not arrive on an interface that is an admin-scope border for its first group address.
sections.plainLanguage: Each teacher has a rank. If a higher-ranked teacher speaks up, the others stay quiet. If nobody higher speaks for a while, you take the job.

sections.title: Candidate-RPs and Building the RP-Set
sections.content:
Every C-RP periodically unicasts a C-RP-Adv message to the BSR of each scope zone it knows about, every C_RP_Adv_Period. When a new BSR is elected, the C-RP MUST send one to three advertisements, each after a small randomized backoff, because the BSR must learn quickly which RPs are active. The recommendation is three. By default the priority is 192. A C-RP being shut down SHOULD send an advertisement with holdtime zero so the BSR removes it at once.

Each advertisement lists group ranges. The C-RP offers each range to the BSR of the smallest scope that contains it, or to the non-scoped BSR if none does. A C-RP MUST NOT send an advertisement with no group ranges.

The BSR accepts a range only if it is the elected BSR for a scope zone containing it, or the elected non-scoped BSR. It keeps a set of group-to-C-RP mappings, each with an expiry timer taken from the advertisement holdtime, and recommends a way to restrict which addresses it accepts advertisements from. It builds the RP-Set from them, and may limit the number of Candidate-RPs. If it sees both BIDIR and PIM-SM candidates for the same range, it MUST include only one protocol, preferring BIDIR by default.

The BSR sends BSMs at the BS_Period interval, and also when the RP-Set changes, but never more often than BS_Min_Interval. RP holdtimes in a BSM MUST be larger than BS_Period and SHOULD be larger than 2.5 times it. A shutting-down BSR should send a BSM with the lowest possible BSR priority to speed up a new election.
sections.plainLanguage: Room owners keep telling the head teacher they are available. If one stops, its entry expires. The head teacher checks the list is sensible and announces it.

sections.title: Forwarding Bootstrap Messages and Helping New Routers
sections.content:
BSMs are forwarded hop by hop: each router builds a new IP packet carrying the whole BSM for every multicast-capable interface with PIM neighbors, including the one the message arrived on. The reason is that routers on a LAN may have inconsistent routing information, and a router might only accept the message after another router re-forwards it. Scoped BSMs are not sent across the admin-scope boundary.

When a new neighbor appears, or a Hello with a new GenID arrives, one router on the LAN (normally the Designated Router) sends it a stored copy of the BSM for each scope zone, after it has sent a triggered Hello. This SHOULD use a No-Forward BSM, which skips the RPF check and is only accepted at startup. For backward compatibility it MAY instead be unicast, which should be configurable.

Finally, the routing protocols (PIM-SM and BIDIR-PIM) decide how the final mapping is computed from the RP-Sets. A router that supports only one of the two protocols MUST NOT ignore ranges marked for the other, and MUST NOT treat them as its own.
sections.plainLanguage: When a new student joins, a helper hands them a copy of the latest list straight away, so they do not have to wait for the next announcement.

sections.title: The Two BSR Message Types
sections.content:
BSR messages are PIM messages with IP protocol number 103. The PIM message type is 4 for Bootstrap and 8 for Candidate-RP-Advertisement. Bootstrap messages are usually multicast with TTL 1 to the ALL-PIM-ROUTERS group (224.0.0.13 for IPv4, ff02::d for IPv6) and use the link-local address of the sending interface as source. C-RP-Adv messages are unicast to the BSR from a domain-wide reachable address.

A Bootstrap message carries a No-Forward bit, a Fragment Tag, a Hash Mask Len, the BSR Priority and BSR Address, followed by one or more group ranges, each with an RP Count and a list of RP addresses with holdtime and priority. The recommended hash mask length is 30 for IPv4 and 126 for IPv6, and the default BSR priority is 64. The BSR Address, groups and RPs MUST all be of the same address family as the packet.

A large BSM can be split into semantic fragments that share the same Fragment Tag. A router replaces the RPs for a group range only once it has received RP Count of them, so a lost fragment affects only the ranges it carried. To remove a range, the BSR includes it with an RP Count of zero for BS_Timeout.

A C-RP-Adv carries a Prefix Count (which MUST NOT be 0), a Priority, a Holdtime that should be 2.5 times C_RP_Adv_Period, the RP address and the group addresses.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two kinds of notes: the head teacher's big announcement of the list, and the short sign-up note a room owner sends to the head teacher.

sections.title: Timers and Default Values
sections.content:
The mechanism is driven by a handful of timers. The defaults are BS_Period of 60 seconds, BS_Timeout of 130 seconds, BS_Min_Interval of 10 seconds and C_RP_Adv_Period of 60 seconds. SZ_Timeout is 1300 seconds, and C_RP_Adv_Backoff is a random value from 0 to 3 seconds.

BS_Timeout MUST be larger than BS_Period, and 2 times BS_Period plus 10 seconds is recommended. SZ_Timeout MUST be larger than BS_Timeout, with 10 times BS_Timeout recommended.

BS_Rand_Override is computed from a formula over the difference in priority and address, and lies between 5 and 23 seconds. A C-BSR with a higher weight gets a smaller value, so the better candidate normally takes over first.
sections.plainLanguage: Everything runs on stopwatches: how often to announce, how long to wait before deciding the head teacher has vanished, and how long to remember a room that stopped answering.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The threats are denial of service and traffic diversion. An attacker who subverts a BSM, or registers as a C-RP, can stop traffic reaching receivers, steer it to a place where it can be monitored, or flood a third party by naming it as the RP.

The recommended defenses are layered. Implementations SHOULD offer a per-interface option to send and accept no Bootstrap messages, which should be set on border routers and on leaf interfaces. Border routers should also drop unicast PIM messages and filter spoofed source addresses. The BSR should restrict which addresses it accepts C-RP-Adv messages from. Unicast BSMs carry extra risk because a router briefly accepts them after a reboot, so supporting them is for backward compatibility only and should be configurable.

Where topology makes this insufficient, the RFC recommends IPsec Authentication Header between PIM routers and IPsec authentication for C-RP-Adv messages. Rate limiting of PIM packets is recommended, and the limiter MUST treat different PIM packet types independently, so a flood of C-RP-Adv messages cannot cause Bootstrap messages to be dropped.
sections.plainLanguage: A fake announcement could send everyone to the wrong room. So routers only listen to neighbors they trust, and they sign the important notes.
